usedCounterFrames: leaders-eat-last-ch01: The mistaken move is to ask exposed people for courage while rank stays clean. The better move is to turn authority into cover first, then ask for truth, speed, or risk.
leaders-eat-last-ch02: The mistake is to add kindness after process has already flattened the person. The better move is to restore one human fact before judgment hardens.
leaders-eat-last-ch03: The weak move is to prove belonging with warmth when nothing is at stake. The stronger move is to correct the mistake while proving membership is not on trial.
leaders-eat-last-ch04: The mistake is treating every yeah-but as cynicism or every deadline as permission to drop safety. The better move is to turn pressure into a design constraint.
leaders-eat-last-ch05: The trap is not ambition itself. It is letting more impersonate responsibility after the purpose has already been served.
leaders-eat-last-ch06: The trap is not low motivation. It is overfeeding quick individual rewards until trust-building rewards feel slow, optional, or invisible.
leaders-eat-last-ch07: The problem is not urgency. It is chronic alarm that keeps people in self-protection after the useful signal is gone.
leaders-eat-last-ch08: The wrong move is to treat rank as earned comfort. The better move is to make privilege match the first burden when the group is under strain.
leaders-eat-last-ch09: Courage is not dramatic boldness. It is accepting the cost that keeps truth and standards from being pushed onto someone weaker.
leaders-eat-last-ch10: The lazy move is to label the person first. The harder move is to test the terrain before deciding whether the person, role, or system is failing.
leaders-eat-last-ch11: The danger is not success itself. It is letting strong results certify habits that will break the group when conditions change.
leaders-eat-last-ch12: The mistake is turning friction into a generation verdict. The better move is to ask what each group was trained to expect before changing the rule.
leaders-eat-last-ch13: The danger is not data. It is letting a category decide after the human cost has disappeared from view.
leaders-eat-last-ch14: The problem is not modern tools. It is using summaries as substitutes for judgment when scale has widened the distance to consequence.
leaders-eat-last-ch15: The failure is not having process. The failure is letting process close before the human fact that could change judgment is found.
leaders-eat-last-ch16: The danger is not measurement. It is letting measurable order win so often that trust, discretion, and judgment lose their place in the system.
leaders-eat-last-ch17: Culture is not the mood people describe. It is the behavior they learn to repeat when pressure makes the values expensive.
leaders-eat-last-ch18: The leader's speech matters less than the first visible reaction everyone can copy when bad news arrives.
leaders-eat-last-ch19: Integrity is not proven by believing the principle. It is proven when the first convenient exception would make life easier.
leaders-eat-last-ch20: Friendship at work is not forced fun or special treatment. It is enough real knowledge for candor and sacrifice to travel safely.
leaders-eat-last-ch21: The mistake is not using numbers. The mistake is letting numbers command the decision before they have led you back to the people and conditions underneath.
leaders-eat-last-ch22: Systems can be real and unfair while your own habit still feeds them. Agency begins where complaint names the benefit you keep taking.
leaders-eat-last-ch23: The problem is not wanting wins. The problem is calling a win clean before you know who carried the hidden bill.
leaders-eat-last-ch24: The wrong move is contempt or excuse. The better move is to ask what conditions trained thin trust, then rebuild standards through concrete trust.
leaders-eat-last-ch25: Admission is not recovery. The better move is to turn the known habit into repeated practice, visible proof, accountability, and help.
leaders-eat-last-ch26: Hardship does not bond people by itself. Trust grows when leaders enter a protected burden instead of outsourcing strain.
leaders-eat-last-ch27: More leaders does not mean more bosses or saviors. It means more people taking local responsibility for protection before permission arrives.
usedTryThisNowFrames: leaders-eat-last-ch01: Before your next correction, write the name of the person most exposed and one sentence you can say that puts the first heat on you.
leaders-eat-last-ch02: Pick one rule you enforce this week and write the human fact it misses before you decide the next correction.
leaders-eat-last-ch03: In the next tense group moment, say the standard that still holds and the membership that is not at risk before the review continues.
leaders-eat-last-ch04: Take one objection you hear today and rewrite it as: how do we keep the standard while reducing the unnecessary threat?
leaders-eat-last-ch05: Choose one active target and write the condition that would make the next increment unnecessary or distorting.
leaders-eat-last-ch06: Look at one scoreboard or incentive and mark whether it rewards chase, status, bonding, or care. Change one signal that crowds out trust.
leaders-eat-last-ch07: Pick one recurring alert, meeting, or metric and ask what threat it keeps broadcasting after the useful signal is gone.
leaders-eat-last-ch08: Name one privilege your role gives you and the matching burden you will take first when pressure rises.
leaders-eat-last-ch09: Write the sentence you are avoiding because it will cost you comfort, then decide who pays if you keep avoiding it.
leaders-eat-last-ch10: Before your next performance judgment, list two terrain factors that would make a capable person fail here.
leaders-eat-last-ch11: Pick one practice currently praised because results are good and ask what behavior it is training if pressure changes.
leaders-eat-last-ch12: When a rule feels obvious to one age group and absurd to another, write what each group was trained to expect before choosing a response.
leaders-eat-last-ch13: Take one anonymous label in a decision and replace it with one concrete person and the consequence they will feel.
leaders-eat-last-ch14: For one dashboard or workflow, add the person or place you will check before acting on the summary.
leaders-eat-last-ch15: Before approving one process-driven decision, ask what human fact would change your mind and go get that fact.
leaders-eat-last-ch16: Look at one metric that is winning every tradeoff and write the invisible human condition it is starving.
leaders-eat-last-ch17: Find one repeated tradeoff everyone notices and write what it teaches people this place really rewards.
leaders-eat-last-ch18: Before responding to bad news, write what your first visible reaction will teach everyone watching.
leaders-eat-last-ch19: Find one standard you believe in and write the exception that will tempt you to bend it this month.
leaders-eat-last-ch20: Ask one person a specific question about the burden they are carrying, then use the answer to change one demand or offer one concrete help.
leaders-eat-last-ch21: Choose one red or green metric and name the person, place, or conversation it should send you toward before you act on it.
leaders-eat-last-ch22: Name one pattern you criticize, then write the small convenience, approval, or relief you get by letting it continue.
leaders-eat-last-ch23: Pick one recent win and write three names: who got credit, who did cleanup, and who paid a cost that stayed offscreen.
leaders-eat-last-ch24: Pick one habit you judge quickly, name the environment that may have trained it, then choose one concrete trust rep that could retrain it.
leaders-eat-last-ch25: Choose one harmful habit you already understand and schedule the next accountable practice that would prove change to someone else.
leaders-eat-last-ch26: Choose one hard task you have been watching from above and take a visible, useful share of the burden this week.
leaders-eat-last-ch27: Name one human cost close enough for you to affect, then take one protective action that does not require a new title.
